newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court upholds O'Dell's death sentence.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court upholds O'Dell's death sentence.

text.p: A sharply divided Supreme Court on Thursday upheld the death sentence for Virginia death-row inmate Joseph O'Dell, whose cause has been championed by capital punishment foes around the world including Pope John Paul II.

The high court, by a 5-4 vote, rejected the convicted murderer's claims that his death sentence should be overturned because he was not allowed to tell his sentencing jury that an alternative to death was life without parole.

At issue was the reach of a 1994 Supreme Court ruling requiring that a capital defendant be allowed to tell the jury about an alternative life-in-prison-without-parole sentence if the prosecutor says the defendant presents a future danger.

Justice Clarence Thomas wrote for the court majority that the 1994 decision does not apply retroactively to cases in which the sentence already has been handed down. O'Dell was sentenced six years earlier.
The "rule was new and cannot therefore be used to disturb (O'Dell's) death sentence," he said in the 16-page opinion.
The Supreme Court did not consider O'Dell's guilt or innocence, only whether he should receive the death penalty or should be resentenced to life in prison.

O'Dell, 55, also has claimed new DNA evidence casts doubt on his 1986 conviction for raping and murdering a 44-year-old secretary from Virginia Beach, Virginia. Lower U.S. courts have rejected those arguments.
His case has been publicised by death penalty opponents on the Internet, sparked street protests in Rome and has drawn the attention of Pope John Paul.
Dissenting from the ruling were the court's most liberal members -- Justices John Paul Stevens, David Souter, Ruth Bader Ginsburg and Stephen Breyer.
Stevens said in the strongly worded dissent that imposition of the death sentence would violate O'Dell's constitutional rights to due process under the law.

"This case is not about whether O'Dell was given a fair sentencing hearing; instead, the question presented is whether, despite the admittedly unfair hearing, he should be put to death because his trial was conducted before (the 1994 decision)," Stevens said.
He said the 1994 decision applied a fundamental principle long present in the U.S. legal system that had been clearly articulated by the high court in two earlier rulings.

Although the high court cleared the way for his execution, O'Dell can appeal to Virginia Gov. George Allen for clemency. Allen had said he would wait for the high court ruling before deciding whether O'Dell should die by lethal injection.
